enrichment.short_title: Tesco employee bribe and share option forfeiture
key_facts: Tesco manager Simon Pook approved false invoices totalling over £512,000 for Universal Projects and was convicted of theft.
Tesco claimed £323,749.99 paid by Delta Computer Systems was a secret bribe used partly to fund a Bishop's Stortford property purchase.
Pook counterclaimed for £51,156.58 under an executive share option scheme exercised after suspension but before dismissal.
Peter Smith J held Pook received a bribe, must account including VAT, and could not exercise share options while in breach of fiduciary duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of residual bribe claim and share option counterclaim in Chancery proceedings after consent judgment on false invoices.
enrichment.outcome: Tesco succeeded on bribe claim and counterclaim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A secret payment from a third party dealing with the employer is a bribe without proof of corrupt motive; the agent holds it on trust for the principal, and an employee in serious breach of fiduciary duty cannot exercise share options while that breach would justify summary dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether proof of motive is required to establish a bribe
Quantum including VAT on bribes held on trust
Implied term preventing exercise of share options during gross misconduct
Positive duty of senior employees to disclose fiduciary breaches

enrichment.short_title: Maersk damages for fraudulent cargo shortage claims
key_facts: Maersk Sealand sought damages for costs defending fraudulent non-delivery and delay claims brought by the Akar family in Hong Kong and Guinea.
In the first claim, customs records indicated the consignees removed textiles from a container before falsely claiming theft and pursuing inflated claims ten times the declared value.
Bills of lading contained exclusive English jurisdiction and anti-suit clauses protecting Maersk and its agents.
At an uncontested trial Flaux J awarded US$130,941.48 plus interest, declarations of fraud, indemnities, and £140,000 costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Uncontested Commercial Court trial under CPR Part 39.3 following worldwide freezing orders.
enrichment.outcome: Claims largely succeeded with damages, declarations, indemnities, and apportioned costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where cargo consignees fraudulently abstract goods and pursue false claims in breach of exclusive jurisdiction and anti-suit clauses in Maersk bills of lading, the carrier may recover reasonable costs of defending foreign proceedings as damages for deceit and/or breach of contract.
legal_issues: Proof of fraud on the balance of probabilities at uncontested trial
Enforcement value of reasoned judgment against absent defendants
Breach of exclusive English jurisdiction clause
Recoverability of foreign litigation costs as contractual damages

enrichment.short_title: Tree root subsidence claims dismissed at Laburnum Grove
key_facts: Two homeowners at Laburnum Grove, Ruislip claimed remedial costs after structural damage to houses adjacent to Ruislip Wood owned by Hillingdon Council.
The council contended damage was caused by heave from re-hydration of desiccated London Clay after pre-development tree removal, not subsidence from woodland oak roots.
Expert evidence conflicted; the court preferred Dr Hope and Mr Billingham over the claimants' experts on causation.
Both the Siddiqui and Sohanpal actions were dismissed after findings that tree roots from the wood did not cause the damage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated TCC trial of two nuisance claims for remedial works after subsidence damage.
enrichment.ratio: Claimants alleging tree-root subsidence must prove causation on the balance of probabilities; where expert evidence shows damage was caused by heave from desiccated clay at construction rather than ongoing root moisture abstraction, nuisance liability does not arise even if foreseeability issues might otherwise be debated.
legal_issues: Subsidence versus heave on London Clay
Proof of causation in tree root nuisance claims
Reasonable foreseeability under Delaware Mansions
Opportunity to abate nuisance before recovery of underpinning costs

enrichment.short_title: Compulsory treatment limited to classified mental disorder
key_facts: A restricted patient detained at Ashworth for manslaughter was classified by tribunal as suffering mental illness, not personality disorder.
Clinicians diagnosed comorbid personality disorder and treated him on a personality disorder ward despite the classification.
The patient sought judicial review of compulsory treatment for an unclassified disorder; Tucker J dismissed the claim.
The Court of Appeal held section 63 authorises compulsory treatment only for the classified mental disorder justifying detention.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from administrative court judicial review of Ashworth Hospital treatment and placement decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; compulsory treatment for unclassified personality disorder held unlawful.
enrichment.ratio: Section 63 of the Mental Health Act 1983 permits treatment without consent only for the mental disorder classified in the hospital order or tribunal decision that justifies detention, not for any clinician-diagnosed disorder; emergency treatment for non-classified disorders may still be available at common law.
legal_issues: Construction of section 63 MHA 1983
Relationship between classification, detention, and treatability
Comorbidity and ancillary treatment
Effect of R v Anglia and Oxfordshire MHRT ex p Hagan

enrichment.short_title: Without prejudice payment letter creates no charge
key_facts: Celtic Contractors sought to continue a freezing injunction over IES funds based on a without-prejudice SAS broker letter governing payments from a Barclays joint account.
The letter proposed monthly certified payments to Celtic from Canary Wharf project receipts but contemplated a formal legal agreement.
Parties had operated under the letter for months before a payment dispute arose.
Mantell LJ upheld refusal to continue the injunction, finding no equitable charge and balance of convenience against freezing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to continue interim freezing injunction pending sub-contract debt trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: A without-prejudice broker letter contemplating a future formal agreement and limiting payment to mutually agreed monthly sums does not, even if binding, create an equitable charge over a third-party bank account sufficient to justify a freezing order; American Cyanamid balance of convenience may also oppose such relief.

enrichment.short_title: Local authority cannot fund return to Jamaica

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: A Jamaican mother and two daughters sought support from Oxfordshire after fleeing domestic abuse and leaving a refuge.
Social Services assessed them under section 17 and offered fares to return to Jamaica, proposing the children rejoin their father and grandparents.
The mother challenged the decision as procedurally flawed and irrational given A's mental health history and lack of welfare evidence from the father.
Maurice Kay J quashed the section 17 decision and ordered continued interim accommodation pending reassessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of local authority section 17 Children Act assessment and repatriation offer.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review succeeded; repatriation decision quashed with interim support continued.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority may discharge section 17 duties by funding return to the home country only where assessment establishes that doing so meets the children's best interests with proper inquiry into family capacity and available support; deciding children should live with their father without contacting him vitiates the decision, and repatriation is inappropriate where Jamaica offers no equivalent welfare safety net.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of section 17 repatriation as discharge of duty
Procedural fairness and consultation with children and family abroad
Rationality of accommodation and support assumptions in Jamaica
Interaction of section 17 with section 21 National Assistance Act

enrichment.short_title: Employer lacked knowledge of psychiatric vulnerability
key_facts: Former town clerk Mrs Croft obtained £197,401 after a disciplinary warning letter triggered a depressive breakdown.
She had long-standing recurrent depression but presented as robust at work and had not pleaded that councillors knew of her psychiatric history.
The trial judge inferred council knowledge from a friend's belief she saw a counsellor, unsupported by witness evidence.
Potter LJ allowed the liability appeal, holding psychiatric vulnerability and foreseeability of breakdown were not established.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with renewed permission application on liability after single judge granted leave on quantum only.
enrichment.outcome: Liability appeal allowed; judgment set aside on breach of duty.
enrichment.ratio: An employer is liable for psychiatric injury from disciplinary action only if it knew the employee was psychiatrically vulnerable and breakdown was reasonably foreseeable; belief that a colleague knew the employee attended counselling, without more, cannot establish knowledge of vulnerability sufficient to meet the Hatton primary-victim test.

enrichment.short_title: BIFA nine-month time bar held reasonable
key_facts: Granville Oil claimed against freight forwarder Davis Turner for transit damage to Kuwait paint and failure to obtain all-risks insurance.
BIFA Standard Trading Conditions clause 30(B) required suit and written notice within nine months.
Underwriters rejected the insurance claim late; the claimant issued proceedings after the nine-month period.
The Court of Appeal held clause 30(B) reasonable and effective to bar the claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issue trial on UCTA reasonableness of BIFA clause 30(B).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; time bar effective to bar claims.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 30(B) of the BIFA Standard Trading Conditions, requiring suit and notice within nine months, is a fair and reasonable time bar between commercial parties of equal bargaining strength for freight forwarding contracts, including failure-to-insure claims, provided the forwarder promptly notifies the customer when cover is rejected.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC misdirected on provocation appeal test
key_facts: Nicholas Farnell was convicted of murder after trial where defence disavowed provocation though the judge left it to the jury in limited terms.
Psychiatric evidence on depression was relevant to provocation but was directed only on diminished responsibility; R v Smith (Morgan) later clarified the law.
The CCRC refused referral, evaluating whether provocation was sufficiently excusable rather than whether the Court of Appeal might find the conviction unsafe.
Mitchell J quashed the CCRC decision and remitted for reconsideration of referral.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Criminal Cases Review Commission refusal to refer murder conviction.
enrichment.outcome: CCRC decision quashed; case remitted for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: The CCRC must apply the 'real possibility' test predictively by asking whether the Court of Appeal might find a conviction unsafe, not substitute its own evaluation of provocation merits; in section 3 Homicide Act cases the Court of Appeal must treat jury primacy with particular caution and cannot simply decide whether the defendant's conduct was excusable.
legal_issues: CCRC real possibility test under section 13 Criminal Appeal Act 1995
Misdirection on provocation at trial
Impact of R v Smith (Morgan) on psychiatric characteristics
Jury primacy in section 3 Homicide Act appeals

enrichment.short_title: Quarry EIA reasons order but permission upheld

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Local residents challenged North Yorkshire's grant of permission to extend sand and gravel quarrying at Ripon City Quarry.
Councillor Paul Richardson was excluded from the planning committee meeting because of a prejudicial interest under the members' code of conduct.
The claim also alleged breach of EIA Regulations for failure to publish main reasons for the decision.
Richards J ordered publication of reasons under reg 21(1) but dismissed the challenge to the permission and code of conduct exclusion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of quarry planning permission and councillor exclusion under Local Government Act 2000 code of conduct.

enrichment.ratio: Failure to make a reg 21(1) EIA statement of main reasons available for public inspection is a procedural breach remediable by mandatory order without quashing permission where environmental information was substantively considered; a councillor with a direct personal interest in a nearby quarry proposal had a prejudicial interest requiring withdrawal even if not on the deciding committee.
